newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-DAVIES RIGHT ABOUT SOLHEIM PUTTING.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-DAVIES RIGHT ABOUT SOLHEIM PUTTING.

text.p: Before this weekend's Solheim Cup between the United States and Europe, world number one Laura Davies said the outcome would depend on "putting, pure and simple."
Purely and simply, the Europeans' putting went to pot on Sunday as the Americans' traditional steel in singles play carried them to a runaway triumph as they retained the trophy.
They overwhelmed Europe 10-2 in the singles to wipe out a two-point overnight deficit and inflict a 17-11 beating.
In victory, the U.S. team avoided the trophy following the Ryder, Walker and Curtis Cups to European side of the Atlantic.

The addition to this Solheim Cup of a second set of foursomes and fourballs, as well as the increase from 10 to 12 singles matches to make it identical to the Ryder Cup, always seemed likely to favour the Americans.
Yet until Sunday, the notion of greater American strength in depth was being exploded.
But in the end it proved to be true and it was also evident that as Davies goes, so goes the European team.
In the opening morning foursomes on Friday when she putted poorly, Davies and her partner lost and the Europeans bowed 3-1/2 to 1/2.
Then for three sets of fourballs and foursomes she could scarcely miss as her side battled back to lead 9-7 by Saturday night.
"For three rounds I had only to look at them and they'd go in. The last day I did not make a putt," the 32-year-old Englishwoman said after losing her singles to Michelle McGann 3 and 2.
Missing three makeable putts on the first four holes, she shot nothing but pars for 13 holes, then two bogeys in three holes finished her off at the 16th.
The Americans seemed to take heart at McGann's victory just as the Europeans sagged.
Few of the home side played well, putted well or forced the Americans to dig deep, despite U.S. captain Judy Rankin's contention afterwards that it had been tough to the very end.
"Until last night we took a whipping. I was not confident we could win today," Rankin said at the finish.

Only Annika Sorenstam of Sweden, one of the few Europeans who have toughened themselves on the U.S. Tour, won a point in the singles. The double U.S. Open champion and world number two beat veteran Pat Bradley 2 and 1 in the opening match.
It ought to have been the start the Europeans needed, but by then too many of them were facing defeat anyway and when Davies could not deliver, the writing was on the wall.
Only Liselotte Neumann of Sweden and Britain's Alison Nicholas could garner half points in draws with Beth Daniel and Kelly Robbins respectively and just two other games went to the last green.
European captain Mickey Walker said the outcome was not a disaster but suggested her pairings in earlier matches might have been different if the first set of foursomes had been closer.
"As a result of that, I had to leave it late to introduce the rookies," she said.
Her tactic of packing the top of the order in the singles with her stronger players did not pay the dividend Walker wanted. "I wanted us to get points on the board quickly," she said.
